Compose runs a group of workers as one project. The Compose daemon reads `worker-compose.yaml`. It
resolves package versions, starts and stops each worker in dependency order, and supervises the
workers while they run.

## The daemon

The daemon is itself a worker. It registers under the name `compose`. Every project operation is a
standard [trigger](./triggers) of one of its `compose::*` functions.

`iii compose` starts the Compose daemon. It reads `worker-compose.yaml` in the working directory and
starts no project workers.

`iii compose --up` is a convenience command. It starts the Compose daemon and the workers in
`worker-compose.yaml`. When the file has an `engine:` section, and you do not set `--engine` or
`III_URL`, it also starts the iii engine. Then it is approximately the same as running `iii`,
`iii compose`, and `iii trigger compose::up` as separate commands. Without an `engine:` section,
`--up` connects to an engine that already runs.

The engine that `--up` starts is tied to the Compose process. If Compose exits for any reason,
including an abrupt kill such as `SIGKILL` during startup, the managed engine is terminated too, and
the next `iii compose --up` starts a fresh engine. An engine that the `iii` command starts has a
lifecycle separate from the Compose process. For process supervision, see
[Deployment](./deployment#run-a-compose-project).

### Starting a project with the daemon

```text
iii compose [OPTIONS]
```

For every option, see the [CLI reference](../cli-reference/index#iii-compose). `--frozen` and
`--file` are valid only with `--up`.

`Ctrl^C`, `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` and `SIGHUP` all gracefully stop the daemon, every worker run by the
daemon, and the iii engine if Compose was started with `--up`. When `--up` has started the engine,
every project and worker stops before the engine process is stopped. `compose::stop` is the function
equivalent of this operation.

Compose only stops an engine it started itself. An external engine, selected with `--engine`,
`III_URL`, or an external engine in the compose file, keeps running when Compose exits. If the
engine's listener port is already in use, `--up` fails. Compose never adopts or kills an unrelated
engine.

`compose::*` functions as documented below are the intended way to manage a running Compose daemon.

### Process names on Linux

Compose includes its resolved namespace in the process label. The daemon uses `iii:c:<namespace>`,
and an engine started by that daemon uses `iii:e:<namespace>`. The namespace comes from
`--namespace`, then `namespace:` in the compose file, then `default`.

For example, `iii compose --namespace orders --up` produces these labels when it starts an engine:

```text
iii:c:orders
  +-- iii:e:orders
```

The process table shows the label in two fields. The `args` field holds the full label and the
original command arguments. The `comm` field holds a short label. Linux limits `comm` to 15 bytes.
In `comm`, a namespace longer than nine characters shows as its first two characters, `~`, and six
hexadecimal hash characters.

The daemon sets its command label through an early re-exec with the same PID, before starting the
runtime or any children. Existing external engines keep their names. On other operating systems,
Compose leaves process names unchanged.

### Compose logs

Compose writes the stdout and stderr of each worker to `logs/` in the
[state directory](#where-compose-keeps-state). The managed engine writes `engine.log` in the same
directory.

Each worker log rotates at 10 MiB. Compose keeps the active file and three archives, so each worker
keeps up to 40 MiB. `engine.log` uses the same limits. Compose removes terminal control sequences
from worker output and engine output before it writes them.

You can use the logs client for a recent snapshot or a live view:

```bash
iii compose logs                         # last 100 lines from every worker
iii compose logs queue --tail 200        # one worker
iii compose logs queue --follow          # keep waiting for new output
iii compose logs queue --stream stderr   # only stderr
iii compose logs queue --namespace dev --engine ws://127.0.0.1:49134
```

For every option, see the [CLI reference](../cli-reference/index#iii-compose-logs).

Each line is prefixed with the worker name, and stderr uses a bold prefix on a terminal.

### Running it in the background

Compose runs in the foreground. It does not send `sd_notify` messages, so a systemd unit uses
`Type=simple`. To run Compose under a process supervisor, see
[Run a Compose project](./deployment#run-a-compose-project).

## The `compose::*` functions

These are the functions that control the Compose daemon and are the canonical way of interacting
with it and making basic changes to the `worker-compose.yaml` file.

| Function             | Takes                                                                   | Returns                                                                                                        |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compose::up`        | `file`, `container`, `frozen`                                           | When the change is complete: `status`, `changed`, and `affected_workers`.                                      |
| `compose::down`      | `file`, `container`                                                     | The same fields as `compose::up`.                                                                              |
| `compose::status`    | `file`                                                                  | The project's namespace, file, state directory, daemon pid, worker states.                                     |
| `compose::logs`      | `file`, `container` or `worker`, `cursors`, `tail`, `stream`, `wait_ms` | Bounded stdout/stderr entries and one cursor per worker.                                                       |
| `compose::list`      | nothing                                                                 | The daemon name, its namespace, its pid, and every project it holds.                                           |
| `compose::validate`  | `file`                                                                  | A validation report.                                                                                           |
| `compose::add`       | `file`, `workers` or `worker`, `operation_id`                           | An accepted operation: `operation_id`, `status: "accepted"`, and `requested`. The edit runs in the background. |
| `compose::remove`    | `file`, `workers` or `worker`, `operation_id`                           | An accepted operation, as for `compose::add`.                                                                  |
| `compose::restart`   | `file`, `container` or `worker`                                         | The same fields as `compose::up`. A restart of one worker also returns `worker`.                               |
| `compose::update`    | `file`, `workers` or `worker`, `operation_id`                           | An accepted operation, as for `compose::add`.                                                                  |
| `compose::operation` | `operation_id`                                                          | A snapshot of the operation: its `status`, `phase`, progress counts, and last event.                           |
| `compose::cancel`    | `operation_id`                                                          | `operation_id` and `cancelled`. `cancelled` is `false` when the daemon has no operation with that id.          |
| `compose::stop`      | nothing                                                                 | The daemon name, its pid, and the projects it is about to stop.                                                |
| `compose::schema`    | `function_id`                                                           | Request/response JSON Schemas, descriptions, timeouts, and retry safety.                                       |

`file` is not required. Left out, it falls back to a `worker-compose.yaml` in the daemon's own
working directory; without one, the call fails with `NO_COMPOSE_FILE`. A relative `file` path is
relative to the working directory of the daemon. You may pass an absolute path as well.

Each call also accepts `namespace`. Compose compares it with its own daemon namespace. When the
values differ, the call fails with `WRONG_DAEMON`. To select a daemon, use `--namespace` on
`iii trigger`.

`compose::up` and `compose::down` read only `container`.

```bash
iii trigger compose::up      --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml
iii trigger compose::up      --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml frozen=true
iii trigger compose::up      --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml container=api
iii trigger compose::status  --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml
iii trigger compose::logs    --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml worker=api tail=100
iii trigger compose::down    --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml
iii trigger compose::list    --namespace dev
iii trigger compose::add     --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml worker=database worker=web
iii trigger compose::remove  --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml worker=state
iii trigger compose::restart --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml
iii trigger compose::schema  --namespace dev function_id=compose::up
iii trigger compose::stop    --namespace dev
```

`iii trigger` waits 30 seconds by default. Its `--timeout-ms` option sets a different wait, in
milliseconds. For every option, see the [CLI reference](../cli-reference/index#iii-trigger).
`compose::status` reports the state of each worker while a project starts.

### Starting a project

`compose::up` starts every worker in the compose file, in dependency order. Workers that are already
ready stay as they are.

Compose starts workers in dependency waves. It starts up to 8 workers at the same time, and it
downloads up to 8 packages at the same time. To change this limit, set
`III_COMPOSE_MAX_PARALLEL_WORKERS` to a positive integer in the environment of the daemon.

| Field       | Description                                                                                  |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`      | The project to start.                                                                        |
| `container` | Starts that worker and the workers it depends on, and nothing else.                          |
| `frozen`    | Requires a current `worker-compose.lock` and does not resolve package selectors when `true`. |

A failed worker fails the operation only when it is required. See
[Required workers](#required-workers).

### Stopping a project

`compose::down` stops the project in reverse dependency order.

| Field       | Description                                                            |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`      | The project to stop.                                                   |
| `container` | Stops that worker and the workers that depend on it, and nothing else. |

### Adding workers

`compose::add worker=state worker=./workers/api` declares one or more workers in the compose file
and reconciles the project once. On the CLI, repeat `worker=` for each worker. Each value takes a
registry package name (`state`), a package name with a version (`state@0.21.4`), or a directory
(`./workers/api`).

The call returns an accepted operation. The edit runs in the background. See
[Following an operation](#following-an-operation).

A `worker=` value can also be a JSON container object. Each object accepts the container fields from
`worker-compose.yaml`. The container key comes from the last part of the worker name or directory
path.

```bash
iii trigger compose::add --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml \
  worker=database \
  worker='{
    "worker": "./workers/api",
    "start_after": ["database"],
    "scripts": {"pre_run": "pnpm build", "pre_run_timeout": "60s", "run": "pnpm start", "post_run": "echo stopped"},
    "config_name": "api",
    "config_override": {"port": 3000},
    "working_dir": "./workers/api",
    "environment": {"NODE_ENV": "development"},
    "env_file": ["./api.env"],
    "startup_timeout": "30s"
  }'
```

| Field          | Description                                                                               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`         | The project to edit.                                                                      |
| `workers`      | A JSON list of worker names or container objects.                                         |
| `worker`       | One worker. Repeatable on the CLI.                                                        |
| `operation_id` | Optional. The id of the operation. See [Following an operation](#following-an-operation). |

A container object accepts these fields:

| Field             | Description                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `worker`          | Required. A package name, `name@version`, registry reference, or local path. Also accepts `package://` and `path://` sources. |
| `version`         | Package version. Must agree with a version included in `worker`.                                                              |
| `start_after`     | Container keys to start first. Compose adds the package's resolved dependencies to this list.                                 |
| `scripts`         | `pre_run`, `pre_run_timeout`, `run`, and `post_run`. `run` is valid only for local workers.                                   |
| `config_name`     | Name of the worker's base configuration.                                                                                      |
| `config_override` | Configuration value applied over the base configuration.                                                                      |
| `working_dir`     | Working directory, relative to the compose file.                                                                              |
| `environment`     | Environment variables with string values.                                                                                     |
| `env_file`        | List of environment file paths, relative to the compose file.                                                                 |
| `startup_timeout` | Maximum wait for worker registration, such as `30s`.                                                                          |

A package without a version pins to the latest available version, for example `0.23.1`. An explicit
selector such as `state@next` stays as `next` in `worker-compose.yaml`.

When a requested registry name is an alias of another package, the daemon writes a warning to its
output and sends it as a progress event with phase `warning`. For example,
`compose::add worker=console` gives
`warning: worker 'console' is an alias of 'ade'. Using container 'console'. Use 'package://api.workers.iii.dev/ade' for new references.`
A worker that you name keeps the container key that you gave. A dependency that is an alias uses the
container key of the canonical package.

Unknown fields and invalid field types are rejected. Compose validates the complete edited file
before it writes any changes.

For an existing container, omitted fields other than `version` keep their values. A supplied field
replaces that entire field, including maps such as `scripts`, `environment`, and `config_override`.
Use `{}` or `[]` to clear maps or lists. An omitted `start_after` keeps existing dependencies; a
supplied list replaces them and includes any required package dependencies.

Workers whose declarations did not change remain running. Existing workers whose source, version,
dependencies, or settings changed restart in place. Newly declared workers start through the normal
dependency plan. If the resolved declaration already matches the file, the call makes no file
changes and causes no restart.

### Removing a worker

`compose::remove worker=state` removes the named worker and every reference to it. The changes are
validated before a worker is removed. Compose then stops only that worker and runs an idempotent
`up`. The call returns an accepted operation. See [Following an operation](#following-an-operation).

| Field          | Description                        |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `file`         | The project to edit.               |
| `worker`       | The worker to remove.              |
| `workers`      | A list of workers to remove.       |
| `operation_id` | Optional. The id of the operation. |

Removal does not resolve the registry graph or remove other workers that were added with this
worker. Those remain declared until they are removed explicitly.

### Restarting one worker

`compose::restart worker=state` stops that specified worker and starts it again. All other workers,
including dependencies, are left unchanged.

`compose::restart` without a worker argument restarts the entire Compose project. It is
approximately the equivalent of `compose::down` followed by `compose::up`.

| Field       | Description                                                    |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`      | The project to restart.                                        |
| `container` | The worker to restart. `worker` is accepted as the same field. |

### Updating workers

`compose::update` without `worker` or `workers` sets `version` to `latest` for every declared
`package://` worker and resolves it. A dependency that `compose::add` wrote, and that another
declared package needs, follows the dependency graph of that package. Compose keeps the registry
reference of each worker and skips `path://` workers. The call returns an accepted operation. See
[Following an operation](#following-an-operation).

```bash
iii trigger compose::update
iii trigger compose::update file=worker-compose.yaml
```

`compose::update worker=state` resolves the selector already in the compose file. A tag such as
`next`, a range, and an exact version all remain unchanged in the file. Use
`worker=state@<selector>` to change the selector. For example, use `worker=state@latest` to move an
exact version to the registry's latest channel.

Update resolves the complete dependency graph. It adds new dependencies, updates changed
dependencies, and removes stale dependencies that Compose generated and no remaining package root
uses. Manually declared workers are not removed.

Compose downloads and verifies the new artifact before it changes the lock or stops a worker. A
failed resolve or download leaves the prior lock and running workers unchanged. If the resolved
artifact and default configuration did not change, Compose updates lock metadata when needed and
does not restart the project.

If all selected workers already use the requested versions, the operation leaves the file and
running processes unchanged. A project with only `path://` workers also stays unchanged.

| Field          | Description                                                       |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`         | The project to edit.                                              |
| `worker`       | Optional worker spec: `name` or `name@version`.                   |
| `workers`      | Optional non-empty list of specs. Takes precedence over `worker`. |
| `operation_id` | Optional. The id of the operation.                                |

```text
worker=state            resolve the selector already declared in the compose file
worker=state@0.21.4     that version, which is also how a downgrade is spelled
worker=state@next       the version currently selected by the next tag
worker=state@latest     the version currently selected by the latest tag
```

The worker has to be declared already in order to be updated, and it has to be a `package://`. Use
[`compose::add`](#adding-workers) to add new workers.

`path://` workers have no version. A change to a `path://` worker takes effect when the worker
restarts.

<Note>
  An update that changes package content or graph topology restarts the whole project once.
</Note>

### Following an operation

`compose::add`, `compose::remove`, and `compose::update` return before the edit is complete. The
response holds `operation_id`, `status: "accepted"`, and `requested`, the number of requested
workers. The daemon runs the edit in the background.

To choose the id yourself, pass `operation_id` in the call. An id that the daemon already holds
fails with `OPERATION_ID_ALREADY_EXISTS`. The daemon keeps each operation until the daemon exits.

```bash
iii trigger compose::add       --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml worker=state operation_id=add-state
iii trigger compose::operation --namespace dev operation_id=add-state
iii trigger compose::cancel    --namespace dev operation_id=add-state
```

`compose::operation` returns a snapshot of the operation:

| Field           | Description                                                         |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `operation_id`  | The id of the operation.                                            |
| `status`        | `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, or `cancelled`.                   |
| `phase`         | The phase of the last event, for example `resolving` or `complete`. |
| `requested`     | The number of requested workers.                                    |
| `total`         | The number of workers in the start plan.                            |
| `completed`     | The number of workers in the plan that settled.                     |
| `last_sequence` | The sequence number of the last event.                              |
| `last_event`    | The last progress event.                                            |

`compose::cancel` asks a running operation to stop. A cancelled operation ends with
`status: cancelled`. Its last event has `terminal: true`. `cancelled` is `true` when the daemon
holds an operation with that id, also when that operation is already complete.

The daemon registers the `compose-operation` trigger type in its namespace. A worker can bind a
trigger of this type to a function. The function then receives each progress event. It receives no
event that the daemon emits before the worker binds the trigger. The trigger follows the call that
has the same `operation_id`. For the binding procedure, see
[Register a trigger](./triggers#register-a-trigger). The trigger configuration takes these fields:

| Field           | Description                                                                               |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `operation_id`  | The operation to follow. Omit it to receive the events of every operation of the daemon.  |
| `terminal_only` | When `true`, the function receives only the last event of the operation. Default `false`. |

Each event has `sequence`, `operation_id`, `phase`, `detail`, `elapsed_ms`, and `terminal`. An event
about one worker also has `container`. An event with progress counts also has `current` and `total`.
The last event has `phase: complete` and `terminal: true`. Compose also calls its own
`compose::operation-progress` function with each event, so each event shows in traces.

### Checking status

`compose::status` reports each declared worker with its `state`, its `version` (the locked package
version, or `local` for a `path://` worker), the active process `pid` when one exists, an `owned`
flag, its rotating `log_path`, and `last_error` when there is one. `owned` is `true` when this
daemon started the worker process and can still stop it. Otherwise `owned` is `false`.

#### Worker states

| State        | Meaning                                                                                          |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `starting`   | Spawned. The engine has not registered it yet.                                                   |
| `ready`      | Registered in the engine under `(namespace, container)`.                                         |
| `restarting` | Waiting for the next configured retry. No process or PID is active.                              |
| `failed`     | Exited unsuccessfully with no eligible retry, exhausted its retries, or one of its hooks failed. |
| `stopped`    | Stopped by the daemon, or exited successfully without an eligible restart.                       |

### Viewing logs

`compose::logs` returns recent stdout and stderr for the workers of one project.

| Field       | Description                                                                                    |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `file`      | The project to read.                                                                           |
| `container` | One worker. Returns every Compose worker when omitted. `worker` is accepted as the same field. |
| `tail`      | Recent lines returned when no cursor is sent. Default 100, maximum 1000.                       |
| `cursors`   | The `cursor` from the last response, keyed by worker. The call continues from there.           |
| `stream`    | `stdout` or `stderr`. Omit for both.                                                           |
| `wait_ms`   | Wait this many milliseconds for new output. Maximum 5000.                                      |

The response holds one entry per worker with `container`, `entries`, `cursor`, and `truncated`. Each
entry in `entries` has `stream` and `message`. A `cursor` has `generation` and `offset`. `truncated`
is `true` when the cursor sent is older than the retained archives.

```bash
iii trigger compose::logs --namespace dev worker=api tail=200
iii trigger compose::logs --namespace dev worker=api stream=stderr wait_ms=5000
```

### Listing projects

`compose::list` returns the daemon name, its namespace, its pid, and other project information.

### Validating a file

`compose::validate` checks a compose file. It takes `file`. Validation does not contact the
registry, so Compose lists `package://` workers in `deferred_packages` and does not resolve them.

#### Validation reports

| Field               | Type   | Description                                               |
| ------------------- | ------ | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `namespace`         | string | Namespace the project's workers register in.              |
| `start_order`       | array  | Worker names in dependency order.                         |
| `deferred_packages` | array  | `package://` workers, which need the registry to resolve. |

### Stopping the daemon

`compose::stop` stops every project of the daemon and their workers. It also stops the engine when
`--up` started that engine. Then the daemon exits. Before it exits, it returns its name, its pid,
and the projects that it will stop. `compose::stop` takes no `container` or `worker`. A call that
names one fails with `STOP_TAKES_NO_CONTAINER`.

<Warning>
  There is no `compose::start` equivalent to `compose::stop`. Stopping a Compose daemon means it
  must be restarted from the server it is running on.
</Warning>

### Viewing schema

`compose::schema` takes a `function_id` argument. With no `function_id`, it returns every
`compose::*` schema. Pass a function id to return the schema for a given function_id. The pseudo-id
`worker-compose.yaml` returns the file's JSON Schema as `request` and a complete small example as
`response`.

Each entry holds `function_id`, `description`, `request`, `response`, `default_timeout_ms`, and
`idempotent`. The same schemas, descriptions, and metadata are also published through
`engine::functions::info`.

```bash
iii trigger compose::schema --namespace dev
iii trigger compose::schema --namespace dev function_id=compose::up
iii trigger compose::schema --namespace dev function_id=worker-compose.yaml
```

## Namespaces

The namespace comes from the `namespace:` field in `worker-compose.yaml` or from the `--namespace`
option at Compose startup. The project's workers receive triggers and function calls only in the
project namespace. For the daemon namespace, project namespace, and routing model, see
[Compose architecture](../understanding-iii/compose). For namespace procedures, see
[Namespaces](./namespaces).

### Precedence

| Value                    | Sets                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-n, --namespace <NS>`   | The daemon namespace, and the project namespace of every project it loads.                                                                                          |
| `namespace:` in the file | The project namespace. For the file that the daemon reads at startup (`./worker-compose.yaml` or `--file`), also the daemon namespace when `--namespace` is absent. |
| Neither                  | `default`.                                                                                                                                                          |

Compose registers its `compose::*` functions in the daemon namespace.

### What a namespace may hold

A namespace contains only lowercase letters `a-z`, digits `0-9`, `-`, and `_`. Any other character,
including an uppercase letter, fails with `INVALID_NAMESPACE`. Compose removes spaces at the start
and end of the value. It does not change an invalid namespace into a valid one.

### One daemon to a namespace

Two Compose daemons with different namespaces can share an engine. However, a second daemon claiming
a namespace that is already served is refused at registration with `DAEMON_ALREADY_SERVING`.

<Warning>
  Only one Compose daemon can serve a namespace on a iii engine. Set `namespace:` in the compose
  file or pass `--namespace` when several daemons must share one iii engine.
</Warning>

## `worker-compose.yaml`

Below is an example compose file. Compose rejects unknown keys and duplicate keys. A duration is a
whole number followed by a unit: `ms`, `s`, or `m`, for example `500ms`, `30s`, or `2m`. A value
without a unit fails with `INVALID_DURATION`.

```yaml
namespace: shop
startup_timeout: 60s
stop_timeout: 10s
engine:
  url: ws://127.0.0.1:49134
  workers:
    configuration:
      adapter:
        name: fs
        config:
          directory: ./config
containers:
  database_1: # Worker names do not need to match package names
    worker: package://database
    version: "0.21.4"
  api:
    worker: path://./workers/api
    start_after: [database_1]
    config_name: shop-api
    config_override:
      log_level: debug
    env_file: [./.env] # specify .envs, later in list overwrites earlier declarations
    environment:
      RUST_LOG: info # specify environment variables directly
      MY_ENV: ${MY_ENV:-defaultValue} # assign an environment variable from the execution environment
    scripts:
      pre_run: npm run migrate
      pre_run_timeout: 2m
      run: npm start
      post_run: ./scripts/cleanup.sh
  state:
    worker: package://state
    version: "0.21.4"
```

### Top-level fields

| Field              | Type    | Default | Description                                                                                   |
| ------------------ | ------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `namespace`        | string  | absent  | Namespace the project's workers register in. A project that declares none lands in `default`. |
| `startup_timeout`  | string  | `60s`   | Readiness budget for every worker. A worker may override it.                                  |
| `stop_timeout`     | string  | `10s`   | Grace between the polite stop and the forced kill.                                            |
| `required_default` | boolean | `false` | Fallback for workers that omit `required`. An explicit worker value wins.                     |
| `engine`           | map     | absent  | Present when this Compose invocation owns and configures the engine.                          |
| `containers`       | map     | empty   | Project workers. May be empty only when `engine:` is present.                                 |

### Engine fields

| Field                             | Type    | Default                | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------- | ------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `url`                             | string  | `ws://127.0.0.1:49134` | Managed engine endpoint used by Compose and its workers. When `engine.workers` has no `iii-worker-manager` entry, the `iii-worker-manager` of the managed engine listens on the host and port of this URL. When that entry exists, its `port` (`49134` when omitted) must match the port of this URL, or the start fails with `MANAGED_ENGINE_ENDPOINT_MISMATCH`. |
| `registration_namespace_grace_ms` | integer | engine default         | Namespace-registration grace passed to the engine.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `workers`                         | map     | empty                  | Direct configs for engine-owned workers. Values must be mappings; use `{}` for defaults.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

Allowed worker keys are `configuration`, `iii-worker-manager`, `iii-http-functions`, `iii-stream`,
and `iii-sandbox`. Use `#instance` for another instance of an allowed type, for example
`iii-worker-manager#rbac`. `configuration` and `iii-worker-manager` always run.
`iii-http-functions`, `iii-stream`, and `iii-sandbox` run only when you declare them. The engine
injects `iii-engine-functions`, `iii-telemetry` for anonymous usage analytics, and
`iii-observability` for OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, and logs. Do not declare these workers. A
declaration under `engine.workers` fails with `ENGINE_WORKER_IS_INJECTED`. When a `compose::add` or
`compose::update` call requests a worker that ships with the engine, its operation fails with
`ENGINE_WORKER_IS_BUILTIN`. Compose leaves out a dependency of this kind.

<Note>Changes to these worker configurations take effect only after the engine restarts.</Note>

#### Which engine Compose uses

Compose takes the engine address from the first of these that supplies one: the `--engine` flag, the
`III_URL` environment variable, the `engine:` section of the compose file, then
`ws://127.0.0.1:49134`.

An address from `--engine` or `III_URL` names an engine that already runs, so Compose connects to it
and starts no engine of its own, even with `--up`. Only the compose file can give Compose an engine
to own, and only `--up` takes it. An `engine:` section holds the whole engine configuration.

Without `--up`, a daemon whose startup file has an `engine:` section connects to the `url` of that
section. It does not start that engine. `--engine` or `III_URL` replaces that address. A daemon that
starts with no `engine:` section connects to an external engine. On that daemon, a call that loads a
compose file with an `engine:` section fails with `ENGINE_SECTION_REQUIRES_MANAGED_START`. Only a
separate `iii compose --up` for that file, with no `--engine` or `III_URL`, loads it. For the
procedure, see [Run a Compose project](./deployment#run-a-compose-project). For the listener port of
a managed engine, see the `url` row in [Engine fields](#engine-fields).

### Worker fields

Each key under `containers` is the name the worker registers under.

| Field             | Type              | Default                                                                         | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `worker`          | string            | required                                                                        | `path://<dir>` or `package://<name>`. A package may name its registry: `package://<registry-host>/<name>`.                                                                                                    |
| `version`         | string            | absent                                                                          | An exact version, a range, or a tag such as `next`. Required for `package://`.                                                                                                                                |
| `start_after`     | array             | empty                                                                           | Workers that must start first. Compose rejects self-dependencies and cycles.                                                                                                                                  |
| `config_name`     | string            | `<namespace>-<container-key>`                                                   | The [configuration worker](./configuration) entry this worker owns.                                                                                                                                           |
| `config_override` | mapping           | absent                                                                          | Merged on top of the fetched configuration; a mapping whose `name` changes is replaced whole.                                                                                                                 |
| `working_dir`     | path              | the worker directory for `path://`, the compose file directory for `package://` | Resolved against the compose file's directory.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `environment`     | map               | empty                                                                           | Environment variables for this worker. Values are strings, booleans, or numbers. A `null` value is left out.                                                                                                  |
| `env_file`        | array of paths    | empty                                                                           | Read at start time, in declaration order. A later file wins on conflicting entries.                                                                                                                           |
| `startup_timeout` | string            | the file's value                                                                | Readiness budget for this worker.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `required`        | boolean           | the file's `required_default`                                                   | Whether a failed start fails the operation. `false` reports the failure and lets the operation carry on. See [Required workers](#required-workers).                                                           |
| `restart`         | string or mapping | `no`                                                                            | What happens after a failed start or a run-time exit. `no`, `on-failure`, `always`, or a mapping with `condition`, `delay`, `max_delay`, `max_attempts`, and `window`. See [Restart policy](#restart-policy). |
| `scripts`         | mapping           | absent                                                                          | See below.                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

`path://` directories resolve against the compose file's directory. A missing directory fails with
`MISSING_WORKER_DIRECTORY`, and a missing `env_file` fails with `MISSING_ENV_FILE` during
validation.

A path worker normally runs as a host process. A non-empty `runtime.base_image` in its
`iii.worker.yaml` makes it run in a local VM. The worker's `scripts.install` and start command then
run inside that image, and Compose keeps the VM state inside the project. An invalid image reference
fails the start.

### Required workers

A worker is not required by default. If it fails to start, its failure is reported against that
worker, nothing is rolled back, and the operation still returns `ok`. Workers that name it in
`start_after` start anyway, because `start_after` sets only the start order. The response lists
every worker that failed this way in `not_required_failures`. A response with `status: ok` has no
top-level `error`; that field is present only when the operation returns `status: failed`.

Set `required: true` when a worker must fail the operation:

```yaml
containers:
  database:
    worker: path://./workers/database
    required: true
```

When a required worker fails to start, Compose stops the workers that the operation started, in
reverse dependency order. `compose::up` returns `status: failed`, and `error.code` holds the code of
the failure, for example `STARTUP_TIMEOUT`. When the first start of `iii compose --up` fails, the
command exits with `PROJECT_DID_NOT_START`. It stops the daemon and the engine that it started.

Use `required_default` to change the fallback for all containers in the file. An explicit container
value wins over the file value:

```yaml
required_default: true

containers:
  queue:
    worker: package://queue
    version: "0.21.9"
    required: false
  state:
    worker: package://state
    version: "0.22.5-rc.1"
```

In this example, `state` inherits `required_default: true`, while `queue` remains false. If both
fields are absent, the effective value is false.

### Restart policy

By default, a failed first start settles immediately. A worker that exits after it was ready takes
its dependents down with it and stays down. To retry either case, declare a restart policy:

```yaml
containers:
  api:
    worker: path://./workers/api
    restart: on-failure
```

`no` is the default. `on-failure` retries a failed start or a worker that exits with a non-zero
status. `always` also restarts it when it exits successfully after it was ready.

The short form uses five attempts, a 500ms base delay, a 30-second maximum delay, and a 60-second
stability window. Use the object form to change these values for one worker:

```yaml
containers:
  api:
    worker: path://./workers/api
    restart:
      condition: on-failure
      delay: 500ms
      max_delay: 30s
      max_attempts: 5
      window: 60s
```

| Field          | Description                                                                     | Default                |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `condition`    | Required in the object form. Accepts `no`, `on-failure`, or `always`.           | `no` in the short form |
| `delay`        | Base delay for exponential backoff after a replacement fails.                   | `500ms`                |
| `max_delay`    | Maximum delay between replacement attempts.                                     | `30s`                  |
| `max_attempts` | Maximum replacement attempts after the original process fails.                  | `5`                    |
| `window`       | Time a ready worker must stay active before its run-time attempt budget resets. | `60s`                  |

The first replacement is immediate. If it fails, later attempts use exponential backoff from `delay`
up to `max_delay`. During `up`, the progress row shows the current attempt and wait. For a run-time
exit, only the named worker bounces: workers that name it in `start_after` keep running and see
their connection drop and reconnect. `compose::status` reports the worker as `restarting` while it
waits for a run-time replacement. Once `max_attempts` is spent, `required` controls whether the
startup operation fails. At run time, the worker is marked `failed`, its dependents are stopped, and
`last_error` says the supervisor gave up.

### Worker kinds

A registry package has a kind. A kind that Compose cannot run fails with `UNSUPPORTED_PACKAGE_KIND`.

| Kind     | How it runs                                                                     |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `binary` | A child process on the host.                                                    |
| `bundle` | A VM. The start command is the bundle's own `scripts.start`, read in the guest. |

A `path://` worker has no package kind. It runs as a host process, or in a local VM when its
`iii.worker.yaml` sets `runtime.base_image`.

Compose boots each VM with `iii-worker`, which the installer puts beside `iii`. On a machine without
`iii-worker`, a VM worker (a bundle, or a path worker with `runtime.base_image`) fails with an error
that says so. Workers that run as host processes are not affected.

Windows has no VM support, so a bundle worker on Windows fails with `BUNDLE_NEEDS_A_VM` before
Compose downloads it. Under WSL, bundle workers run when `/dev/kvm` and a guest rootfs are
available. Workers that run as host processes run on Windows. For Windows setup, see
[Install](../install).

To refuse bundle workers on a machine, set `III_BUNDLE_WORKERS_DISABLED=1`.

### Scripts

| Field             | Type   | Default | Description                                         |
| ----------------- | ------ | ------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `pre_run`         | string | absent  | Runs to completion before the worker is spawned.    |
| `pre_run_timeout` | string | `60s`   | Budget for `pre_run`. Rejected without a `pre_run`. |
| `run`             | string | absent  | Start command. Rejected for `package://` workers.   |
| `post_run`        | string | absent  | Runs after the worker's exit is confirmed.          |

Both hooks run with the worker's environment, working directory, and their own process group. A
`post_run` runs after the worker stops. The daemon waits for it before it exits. `stop_timeout`
applies to each worker: Compose sends a polite stop and waits up to `stop_timeout` before it kills
the worker. A `post_run` also has up to `stop_timeout` to finish.

A path worker's start command is `scripts.run` in `worker-compose.yaml`, or `scripts.start` in the
worker's own `iii.worker.yaml` when `run` is absent. A worker with neither fails with
`MISSING_START_COMMAND`.

### Configuration precedence

Lowest to highest: the configuration a package ships, the entry in the configuration worker, then
`config_override`. Maps merge key by key. Arrays and scalars replace. When the override changes the
`name` of a mapping, the override replaces the whole mapping. Before each start, Compose reads the
entry with `configuration::get` and `raw: true`, applies the override, and writes the result with
`configuration::set` and `flush: false`. The saved entry does not change. When you remove a field
from `config_override`, the field keeps its current value. A read or write failure stops the start
with `CONFIG_FETCH_FAILED`. For `flush` and unsaved values, see [Configuration](./configuration).

### Readable configuration names and migration

Without `config_name`, the entry id is `<namespace>-<container-key>`, for example `default-harness`.
The id must match `[a-z0-9_-]{1,64}`. Compose rejects a generated id that does not match with
`INVALID_CONFIG_NAME`. An explicit `config_name` replaces the generated id. A generated id that is
the same as the explicit `config_name` of another container in the project fails with
`CONFIG_NAME_COLLISION`. Two containers can share an entry only when both set `config_name`.
Different namespaces can produce the same id: namespace `a-b` with key `c` and namespace `a` with
key `b-c` both give `a-b-c`. An explicit `config_name` keeps them apart.

Compose migrates only generated ids. Before a worker starts, Compose calls `configuration::migrate`
to move an entry with the hashed id of earlier versions, such as `default-harness-a14f3656efb8d5ea`,
to the readable id. In the `default` namespace, it also moves an entry named with the bare container
key: `state` becomes `default-state`. Compose skips this move when another container sets
`config_name` to that key. When the destination already exists, the moved entry replaces it, and the
adapter does not back up the replaced destination. The filesystem adapter keeps the old source file
as `<source>.yaml.bak`. Migration requires a configuration worker that supports
`configuration::migrate`. When the configuration worker does not support it, the start fails with
`CONFIG_MIGRATION_FAILED`. Two configuration workers on the same directory during migration are
unsupported. For the upgrade procedure, see
[Preserve stored configuration](../upgrading/workers-to-compose#preserve-stored-configuration).

## The worker environment

A worker's environment combines the following sources, from lowest to highest precedence:

1. The machine environment visible to the Compose daemon. Variables are inherited even when neither
   `env_file` nor `environment` is declared. Non-Unicode names and values are skipped.
2. The worker's `env_file` entries, in declaration order. Later files override earlier files.
   Compose ignores an entry with an empty value, such as `KEY=`, `KEY=""`, or `KEY=''`. For each
   file with empty entries, Compose prints a warning that lists the keys and tells which source
   supplies each key. The warning does not show values.
3. The worker's `environment` map. Nonempty values override env files; an empty string preserves an
   existing env-file value, or supplies an empty value when no env file defines the key.
4. The reserved variables, which the daemon owns.

The daemon captures the machine environment when it starts. A change to the environment of another
shell does not update a running daemon. Workers and hooks inherit the daemon's Unicode machine
variables, including credentials, subject to the daemon-owned values above and the project identity
exception below. Every worker and hook that the daemon starts can read these credentials.

`III_HOST_USER_ID` is not inherited from the machine: it comes from the current project's
`.iii/project.ini`, or is absent when the project has no device ID. A nonempty `env_file` value or
an `environment` value overrides it. Only `environment` can set it to an empty value.

| Variable                | Value                                                                           |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `III_URL`               | The engine address the daemon is connected to.                                  |
| `III_NAMESPACE`         | The project's namespace.                                                        |
| `III_COMPOSE_NAMESPACE` | The supervising Compose daemon's namespace for explicit `compose::*` routing.   |
| `III_COMPOSE_FILE`      | Canonical path of the compose file that owns this worker.                       |
| `III_COMPOSE_DIR`       | Canonical directory that contains the owning compose file.                      |
| `III_WORKER_NAME`       | The key under `containers`.                                                     |
| `III_CONFIG_NAME`       | The explicit configuration id or `<namespace>-<container-key>`, always present. |

Declaring a reserved variable in `environment` or an `env_file` fails with `RESERVED_ENV_OVERRIDE`.
Declaring `III_CONFIG` in `environment` or an `env_file` fails with `RETIRED_CONFIG_ENV`. Compose
removes an `III_CONFIG` value that the daemon inherits from the machine environment.

### Expanding values from environment variables

Compose expands `${VAR}` references in every value except `config_override` and `engine.workers`.
For example:

```yaml
containers:
  queue:
    worker: path://${WORKERS_DIR}/queue
    environment:
      RUST_LOG: ${RUST_LOG:-info}
```

| Written        | Means                                                                                            |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `${VAR}`       | The value from the environment of Compose. Unset, the file is refused with `UNDEFINED_VARIABLE`. |
| `${VAR:-text}` | The value, or `text` when it is unset. `${VAR:-}` makes it optional and empty.                   |
| `$VAR`         | Nothing. A bare name is left alone, so a `scripts.run` holding `$PWD` still reaches the shell.   |
| `$${VAR}`      | A literal `${VAR}`.                                                                              |

<Warning>
  Compose passes `config_override` and `engine.workers` values unchanged. The engine expands
  `${VAR:default}` in `engine.workers` when it loads its configuration. An unset variable with no
  default stops the engine from starting. When a worker reads its entry with `configuration::get`
  without `raw: true`, the configuration worker expands `${VAR}` and `${VAR:default}` from the
  environment of the engine process. An unset variable with no default makes the read fail with
  `EXPAND_FAILED`. These references use `${VAR:default}`, without the `-` that Compose uses.

```yaml
config_override:
  # Expanded from the engine environment when the worker reads its configuration.
  api_key: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}
```

</Warning>

## Packages and the lock

### Package lock

Compose writes a lock file beside the compose file. The lock file has the name of the compose file
with the extension `.lock`, for example `worker-compose.lock`. The compose file keeps the requested
selector. The lock keeps the resolved dependency graph, versions, package types, artifact URLs,
SHA-256 digests, and default configuration returned by the registry.

```text
worker-compose.yaml: next
          |
          v
worker-compose.lock: 0.22.8 + SHA-256
          |
          v
package cache: verified artifact
```

Normal starts and restarts use the lock without resolving `next` again. If the cache is empty,
Compose downloads the URL in the lock and verifies its SHA-256 digest. Compose also verifies the
extracted cache contents before reuse. A changed cache entry is downloaded again from the locked
URL.

`iii compose build --frozen` requires the compose file and lock to match.
`iii compose --up --frozen` and `compose::up frozen=true` apply the same rule during startup. Frozen
mode never resolves selectors or changes the lock. It can download a missing artifact only from the
URL already in the lock. Every environment that uses the same lock gets the same package content.

### Build registry packages

```text
iii compose build [-f, --file <PATH>] [--frozen]
```

For every option, see the [CLI reference](../cli-reference/index#iii-compose-build).

`build` reads and validates the compose file, prepares `worker-compose.lock`, then downloads every
`package://` worker into the same cache used by `compose::up`. The file defaults to
`./worker-compose.yaml`. The command does not connect to an engine, start a worker, or run lifecycle
hooks. Local `path://` workers and the workers under `engine.workers` need no registry download.
`build` skips them.

```bash
iii compose build --file worker-compose.yaml
iii compose build --file worker-compose.yaml --frozen
iii compose --up --file worker-compose.yaml --frozen
```

The cache is shared under `~/.iii/compose/packages`, or under `$III_COMPOSE_STATE_DIR/packages` when
that variable is set. A later `compose::up` reuses a valid cached artifact if it exists.

## Readiness

A worker is considered up when the engine reports a worker of that name in the project's namespace.
Compose polls `engine::workers::list` every 200 ms until the worker's `startup_timeout` runs out.

| Outcome                                                      | Code                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| The worker never appeared.                                   | `STARTUP_TIMEOUT`                  |
| The process exited while Compose was waiting.                | `CHILD_EXITED_BEFORE_REGISTRATION` |
| It registered in `default`, outside the project's namespace. | `WORKER_IGNORED_NAMESPACE`         |
| It registered under a different name in the right namespace. | `WORKER_NAME_MISMATCH`             |
| Its functions landed outside the project's namespace.        | `FUNCTIONS_IN_WRONG_NAMESPACE`     |
| A worker already held that name in the namespace.            | `CONTAINER_NAME_TAKEN`             |

After a worker is ready, the daemon checks it every 250 ms. Its restart policy determines what
happens after it exits. An eligible retry keeps its dependents running and reports `restarting`
between attempts. A successful exit without an eligible retry is recorded as `stopped`. An
unsuccessful exit without an eligible retry, or one that exhausts its retries, is recorded as
`failed`. When no retry remains, its transitive dependents stop. When the engine connection drops
and comes back, every running worker gets its `startup_timeout` to register again.

What stops after a failure depends on when the failure occurs:

| When                                             | What comes down                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| During `up`, a required worker fails             | The operation ends. Compose stops everything the operation started, in reverse order. Workers later in the start order do not start.         |
| During `up`, a worker that is not required fails | Only that worker. Compose lists it in `not_required_failures` and starts the other workers, including workers that name it in `start_after`. |
| After the worker is ready                        | Its transitive dependents. Everything else keeps running.                                                                                    |

## Where compose keeps state

Compose state is stored in `<project-dir>/.iii/compose/<namespace>/`. `<project-dir>` is the
directory containing the canonical compose file, including when `--file` points outside the current
working directory or follows a symbolic link. `<namespace>` is the daemon's namespace.

| Path                 | Contents                                                                                       |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `engine.lock`        | Lock for the managed engine in this project and namespace.                                     |
| `engine-config.yaml` | Generated engine configuration, removed after clean shutdown.                                  |
| `engine.log`         | Rotating stdout and stderr for the managed engine.                                             |
| `state.json`         | Child process records for the project. Owner-only.                                             |
| `logs/`              | Rotating stdout and stderr for project workers.                                                |
| `vm/`                | VM state for bundle and local-image workers, including rootfs, boot scripts and guest configs. |

Two projects can use `default` with separate engines on different ports. Starting the same project
and namespace twice is refused. Two daemons on the same engine must use different namespaces. With
the default state layout, two compose files in the same directory must also use different
namespaces.

`III_COMPOSE_STATE_DIR` moves project state to another directory, for example a writable directory
for a read-only project. Project state is then stored at
`$III_COMPOSE_STATE_DIR/<project-slug>/<namespace>/`. The slug combines the project directory name
with a hash of the canonical compose file path, keeping projects with the same directory name
separate. With this override, two compose files in the same directory have separate state
directories and can use the same namespace on separate engines.

The `.iii/compose/` directory holds generated state. Each nested project has its own `.iii/compose/`
directory.

```bash
iii trigger compose::status --namespace dev file=./worker-compose.yaml
# ... "state_dir": "/home/you/shop/.iii/compose/dev"
ls /home/you/shop/.iii/compose/dev/logs/
```

The per-project layout does not migrate process records or logs from the earlier shared namespace
layout. State from the shared layout stays under `~/.iii/compose/<namespace>/`, or in the old
`III_COMPOSE_STATE_DIR` layout. Compose does not read that state. It has no record of daemons,
engines, or workers that an earlier version started.

## Error codes

Compose can output the following error codes:

| Area                | Codes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Compose file        | `COMPOSE_FILE_UNREADABLE`, `INVALID_COMPOSE_FILE`, `EMPTY_CONTAINERS`, `INVALID_DURATION`, `UNKNOWN_DEPENDENCY`, `SELF_DEPENDENCY`, `DEPENDENCY_CYCLE`, `UNSUPPORTED_WORKER_SOURCE`, `UNDEFINED_VARIABLE`, `INVALID_REFERENCE`, `UNTERMINATED_REFERENCE`                                                                                                        |
| Worker declaration  | `MISSING_VERSION_FOR_PACKAGE`, `RUN_NOT_ALLOWED_FOR_PACKAGE`, `NOT_A_PACKAGE_CONTAINER`, `PRE_RUN_TIMEOUT_WITHOUT_PRE_RUN`, `RESERVED_ENV_OVERRIDE`, `MISSING_ENV_FILE`, `RETIRED_CONFIG_ENV`, `INVALID_CONFIG_NAME`, `CONFIG_NAME_COLLISION`                                                                                                                   |
| Worker resolution   | `MISSING_WORKER_DIRECTORY`, `MISSING_START_COMMAND`, `INVALID_MANIFEST`, `INVALID_WORKER_SPEC`, `WORKER_SOURCE_CHANGED`, `ENGINE_WORKER_IS_BUILTIN`                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| Packages            | `REGISTRY_UNREACHABLE`, `PACKAGE_NOT_RESOLVED`, `PACKAGE_NOT_INSTALLED`, `PACKAGE_DOWNLOAD_FAILED`, `PACKAGE_DIGEST_MISMATCH`, `PACKAGE_ARTIFACT_EMPTY`, `REGISTRY_NAME_REFUSED`, `UNSUPPORTED_PACKAGE_KIND`, `UNSUPPORTED_PLATFORM`, `BUNDLE_NEEDS_A_VM`                                                                                                       |
| Package lock        | `INVALID_COMPOSE_LOCK`, `COMPOSE_LOCK_REQUIRED`, `COMPOSE_LOCK_OUT_OF_DATE`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Start and readiness | `SPAWN_FAILED`, `HOOK_SPAWN_FAILED`, `HOOK_FAILED`, `HOOK_TIMEOUT`, `STARTUP_TIMEOUT`, `CHILD_EXITED_BEFORE_REGISTRATION`, `WORKER_IGNORED_NAMESPACE`, `WORKER_NAME_MISMATCH`, `FUNCTIONS_IN_WRONG_NAMESPACE`, `CONTAINER_NAME_TAKEN`, `CONFIG_FETCH_FAILED`, `CONFIG_MIGRATION_FAILED`, `ENGINE_CALL_FAILED`, `PROJECT_DID_NOT_START`                          |
| Managed engine      | `ENGINE_SECTION_REQUIRES_MANAGED_START`, `ENGINE_ALREADY_OWNED`, `ENGINE_RESTART_REQUIRED`, `ENGINE_WORKER_IS_INJECTED`, `UNSUPPORTED_ENGINE_WORKER`, `INVALID_ENGINE_WORKER_CONFIG`, `INVALID_MANAGED_ENGINE_URL`, `MANAGED_ENGINE_ENDPOINT_MISMATCH`, `MANAGED_ENGINE_LISTENER_UNAVAILABLE`, `ENGINE_SPAWN_FAILED`, `ENGINE_STARTUP_TIMEOUT`, `ENGINE_EXITED` |
| Daemon and project  | `NO_COMPOSE_FILE`, `WRONG_DAEMON`, `INVALID_NAMESPACE`, `UNKNOWN_CONTAINER`, `INVALID_STATE_FILE`, `STATE_DIR_UNAVAILABLE`, `DAEMON_ALREADY_SERVING`, `DAEMON_NAMESPACE_TAKEN`, `STOP_TAKES_NO_CONTAINER`, `IO_ERROR`                                                                                                                                           |
| Operations          | `OPERATION_ID_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `OPERATION_CANCELLED`, `ADD_PLAN_STALE`, `COMPOSE_MUTATION_ROLLBACK_FAILED`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| Command line        | `FILE_REQUIRES_UP`, `FROZEN_REQUIRES_UP`, `BUILD_CONFLICTS_WITH_SERVE_OPTIONS`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

`ENGINE_WORKER_IS_BUILTIN` means that `compose::add` or `compose::update` resolved a requested
registry package of kind `engine`. That worker ships with the engine. To configure an engine-owned
worker (`configuration`, `iii-worker-manager`, `iii-http-functions`, `iii-stream`, or
`iii-sandbox`), use `engine.workers`. See [Engine fields](#engine-fields). Do not declare
`iii-engine-functions`, `iii-telemetry`, or `iii-observability`. The engine injects them.
